One logged work set, or one planned set. Each bout has an id; a standard set is one segment. A drop set is one bout. Its stages are segments, each with its own load and reps. It is never counted as several sets.

A muscle counts a bout once. Two categories from one bout make it `mixed`, with the parts listed. A two-handed bout counts once for each arm (3 sets are 3 per arm, not 6). A one-arm bout counts for that arm only. A bout whose side is unknown is reported separately and never added to either arm.
The muscle performs the movement through its range in this exercise (a reviewed direct, dynamic mapping).
The muscle helps move the load but is not the main target (a reviewed contributing, dynamic mapping).
The muscle holds against load in an exercise whose purpose is the hold (hangs, carries, pinches).
The muscle holds or steadies while something else is trained (gripping a bar during a row).
One set loads the muscle in two different ways; it counts once here, with the parts listed.
The mapping exists but its relationship or muscle action is not known.

Grip credit that needs a bare hand is not given to a set logged with straps. Unknown straps keep the credit and say so. Hold seconds are summed per segment and reported as seconds. They are never converted into sets.

Work tagged with the region in the exercise catalog but with no reviewed atlas mapping counts only at region level, never as work for a specific muscle. Draft mappings are shown as pending review and not counted. Unknown is never shown as zero. The region total counts distinct bouts that touched any of its muscles on that arm. It is not the sum of the muscle rows.

Not counted: Sets not logged as completed (typed but not logged, or skipped). Sets marked as warm-ups. Workouts not finished (the live workout's sets count once it is finished). Removed workouts and sets (they no longer exist on the device).
Load × reps is external volume-load, not muscle force.
Effort that was not recorded stays unknown; it never defaults to failure.
Incidental grip is never counted as dynamic work.
No number here predicts growth, recovery or injury.

Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.

muscle: Brachioradialis: Thumb side of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist; the outermost muscle on that edge.
Bends your elbow. It works whichever way the palm faces; anatomy texts describe it as strongest with the thumb pointing up.
Main action · Bends the elbow, bringing the hand toward the shoulder.

Contributes to the thumb-side contour of the upper forearm, the bulge just below the elbow. It does not bend the wrist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
Studies disagree on whether turning the palm up, sideways or down changes how hard it works in a curl.
From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up; that is not counted as a separate action here.

Hammer-style curls keep the forearm in neutral, where the brachioradialis lies well placed to flex the elbow, and they are the usual choice to train it, so it is a direct target here. EMG studies disagree on how much its activity changes with forearm position (M1 found the change in pronation), so 'direct' is a judgement about the exercise's purpose, not a measured larger share.

Brachioradialis bends the elbow and is active whether the palm faces up, sideways or down. Anatomy references describe it as strongest with the forearm half-turned (thumb up). From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up. It does not cross the wrist.
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Brachioradialis Muscle (Lung, Ekblad, Bisogno) · Structure and Function
Seen through web-search excerpts of the page, not the full text.
Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: brachioradialis · Quick Facts: Action
Relays Gray's Anatomy; a textbook statement, not a measurement.

Whether forearm position changes how hard the brachioradialis works when bending the elbow is unsettled. A surface-EMG study of 16 people found its share differed with the palm down compared with palm up or thumb up; a fine-wire EMG study of 10 people found no difference between the three positions. Neither study measured growth.
Kleiber, Kunz and Disselhorst-Klug, Muscular coordination of biceps brachii and brachioradialis in elbow flexion with respect to hand position (Frontiers in Physiology, 2015) · Abstract: Results
Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Surface electrodes; slow single repetitions.
The function of brachioradialis (University of Kentucky publication record) · Record summary
Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Authors and journal not confirmed by the search.

Brachioradialis is the most superficial muscle on the thumb side of the forearm and forms the fleshy bulge in its upper half, so it may contribute to the thumb-side contour just below the elbow. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

Flexor digitorum superficialis is the main muscle bending the four fingers at their middle (PIP) joints. It also helps bend the knuckles (MCP) and the wrist. It has a separate part, with its own tendon, for each finger.
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle · Introduction; Structure and Function
Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: flexor digitorum superficialis · Quick Facts: Action

The finger parts of FDS can be recruited selectively to some degree, with coupling between fingers. When one finger flexed at half its maximum force, fewer than half of the motor units serving the other fingers' parts became active, and units serving a neighbouring finger were recruited most readily. This supports describing finger actions; it does not show that one finger's part can be trained in isolation.

Butler, Kilbreath, Gorman and Gandevia, Selective recruitment of single motor units in human flexor digitorum superficialis muscle during flexion of individual fingers (Journal of Physiology, 2005) · Abstract
Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Single-motor-unit recordings during isometric finger flexion in healthy adults.

Ordinary gym grip and finger-flexion exercises load FDS together with the deep finger flexor (FDP). In a video-EMG study of fist making, FDP did most of the work in a light fist and FDS joined in every tight fist, in an order that differed between people. No ordinary exercise has been shown to split the work between them, so the atlas shows it as shared and invents no split.

One logged work set, or one planned set. Each bout has an id; a standard set is one segment. A drop set is one bout. Its stages are segments, each with its own load and reps. It is never counted as several sets.

A muscle counts a bout once. Two categories from one bout make it `mixed`, with the parts listed. A two-handed bout counts once for each arm (3 sets are 3 per arm, not 6). A one-arm bout counts for that arm only. A bout whose side is unknown is reported separately and never added to either arm.
The muscle performs the movement through its range in this exercise (a reviewed direct, dynamic mapping).
The muscle helps move the load but is not the main target (a reviewed contributing, dynamic mapping).
The muscle holds against load in an exercise whose purpose is the hold (hangs, carries, pinches).
The muscle holds or steadies while something else is trained (gripping a bar during a row).
One set loads the muscle in two different ways; it counts once here, with the parts listed.
The mapping exists but its relationship or muscle action is not known.

Grip credit that needs a bare hand is not given to a set logged with straps. Unknown straps keep the credit and say so. Hold seconds are summed per segment and reported as seconds. They are never converted into sets.

Work tagged with the region in the exercise catalog but with no reviewed atlas mapping counts only at region level, never as work for a specific muscle. Draft mappings are shown as pending review and not counted. Unknown is never shown as zero. The region total counts distinct bouts that touched any of its muscles on that arm. It is not the sum of the muscle rows.

Not counted: Sets not logged as completed (typed but not logged, or skipped). Sets marked as warm-ups. Workouts not finished (the live workout's sets count once it is finished). Removed workouts and sets (they no longer exist on the device).
Load × reps is external volume-load, not muscle force.
Effort that was not recorded stays unknown; it never defaults to failure.
Incidental grip is never counted as dynamic work.
No number here predicts growth, recovery or injury.

Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.

muscle: Brachioradialis: Thumb side of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist; the outermost muscle on that edge.
Bends your elbow. It works whichever way the palm faces; anatomy texts describe it as strongest with the thumb pointing up.
Main action · Bends the elbow, bringing the hand toward the shoulder.

Contributes to the thumb-side contour of the upper forearm, the bulge just below the elbow. It does not bend the wrist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
Studies disagree on whether turning the palm up, sideways or down changes how hard it works in a curl.
From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up; that is not counted as a separate action here.

Hammer-style curls keep the forearm in neutral, where the brachioradialis lies well placed to flex the elbow, and they are the usual choice to train it, so it is a direct target here. Brachioradialis bends the elbow and is active whether the palm faces up, sideways or down. Anatomy references describe it as strongest with the forearm half-turned (thumb up). From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up. It does not cross the wrist.
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Brachioradialis Muscle (Lung, Ekblad, Bisogno) · Structure and Function
Seen through web-search excerpts of the page, not the full text.
Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: brachioradialis · Quick Facts: Action
Relays Gray's Anatomy; a textbook statement, not a measurement.

Whether forearm position changes how hard the brachioradialis works when bending the elbow is unsettled. A surface-EMG study of 16 people found its share differed with the palm down compared with palm up or thumb up; a fine-wire EMG study of 10 people found no difference between the three positions. Neither study measured growth.

Brachioradialis is the most superficial muscle on the thumb side of the forearm and forms the fleshy bulge in its upper half, so it may contribute to the thumb-side contour just below the elbow. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

muscle: Flexor digitorum superficialis: Palm side, middle layer: under the surface wrist flexors and over the deep finger flexor.
Bends your four fingers at their middle joints, and helps bend the knuckles and the wrist. Each finger has its own part of the muscle, but the parts do not work fully apart.
Main action · Bends the four fingers at their middle joints.
Helps · Bends the four fingers at the knuckles.
Helps · Bends the wrist toward the palm.
May add to the general fullness of the palm side of the forearm. It lies under other muscles, so it has no separately visible outline.
Grip and finger-curl work loads it together with the deep finger flexor (FDP); how the work splits between them is not known.

Flexor digitorum superficialis is the main muscle bending the four fingers at their middle (PIP) joints. It also helps bend the knuckles (MCP) and the wrist. It has a separate part, with its own tendon, for each finger.

Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: flexor digitorum superficialis · Quick Facts: Action

The finger parts of FDS can be recruited selectively to some degree, with coupling between fingers. When one finger flexed at half its maximum force, fewer than half of the motor units serving the other fingers' parts became active, and units serving a neighbouring finger were recruited most readily. This supports describing finger actions; it does not show that one finger's part can be trained in isolation.

Butler, Kilbreath, Gorman and Gandevia, Selective recruitment of single motor units in human flexor digitorum superficialis muscle during flexion of individual fingers (Journal of Physiology, 2005) · Abstract
Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Single-motor-unit recordings during isometric finger flexion in healthy adults.

Ordinary gym grip and finger-flexion exercises load FDS together with the deep finger flexor (FDP). In a video-EMG study of fist making, FDP did most of the work in a light fist and FDS joined in every tight fist, in an order that differed between people. No ordinary exercise has been shown to split the work between them, so the atlas shows it as shared and invents no split.

One logged work set, or one planned set. Each bout has an id; a standard set is one segment. A drop set is one bout. Its stages are segments, each with its own load and reps. It is never counted as several sets.

A muscle counts a bout once. Two categories from one bout make it `mixed`, with the parts listed. A two-handed bout counts once for each arm (3 sets are 3 per arm, not 6). A one-arm bout counts for that arm only. A bout whose side is unknown is reported separately and never added to either arm.
The muscle performs the movement through its range in this exercise (a reviewed direct, dynamic mapping).
The muscle helps move the load but is not the main target (a reviewed contributing, dynamic mapping).
The muscle holds against load in an exercise whose purpose is the hold (hangs, carries, pinches).
The muscle holds or steadies while something else is trained (gripping a bar during a row).
One set loads the muscle in two different ways; it counts once here, with the parts listed.
The mapping exists but its relationship or muscle action is not known.

Draft mappings are shown as pending review and not counted. Unknown is never shown as zero. The region total counts distinct bouts that touched any of its muscles on that arm. It is not the sum of the muscle rows.

Not counted: Sets not logged as completed (typed but not logged, or skipped). Sets marked as warm-ups. Workouts not finished (the live workout's sets count once it is finished). Removed workouts and sets (they no longer exist on the device).

Effort that was not recorded stays unknown; it never defaults to failure.
Incidental grip is never counted as dynamic work.

Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.

muscle: Brachioradialis: Thumb side of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist; the outermost muscle on that edge.
Bends your elbow. It works whichever way the palm faces; anatomy texts describe it as strongest with the thumb pointing up.
Main action · Bends the elbow, bringing the hand toward the shoulder.

Contributes to the thumb-side contour of the upper forearm, the bulge just below the elbow. It does not bend the wrist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
Studies disagree on whether turning the palm up, sideways or down changes how hard it works in a curl.
From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up; that is not counted as a separate action here.

Brachioradialis bends the elbow and is active whether the palm faces up, sideways or down. Anatomy references describe it as strongest with the forearm half-turned (thumb up). From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up. It does not cross the wrist.

Whether forearm position changes how hard the brachioradialis works when bending the elbow is unsettled. A surface-EMG study of 16 people found its share differed with the palm down compared with palm up or thumb up; a fine-wire EMG study of 10 people found no difference between the three positions. Neither study measured growth.

The finger parts of FDS can be recruited selectively to some degree, with coupling between fingers. When one finger flexed at half its maximum force, fewer than half of the motor units serving the other fingers' parts became active, and units serving a neighbouring finger were recruited most readily. This supports describing finger actions; it does not show that one finger's part can be trained in isolation.

Butler, Kilbreath, Gorman and Gandevia, Selective recruitment of single motor units in human flexor digitorum superficialis muscle during flexion of individual fingers (Journal of Physiology, 2005) · Abstract
Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Single-motor-unit recordings during isometric finger flexion in healthy adults.

Ordinary gym grip and finger-flexion exercises load FDS together with the deep finger flexor (FDP). In a video-EMG study of fist making, FDP did most of the work in a light fist and FDS joined in every tight fist, in an order that differed between people. No ordinary exercise has been shown to split the work between them, so the atlas shows it as shared and invents no split.

One logged work set, or one planned set. Each bout has an id; a standard set is one segment. A drop set is one bout. Its stages are segments, each with its own load and reps. It is never counted as several sets.

A muscle counts a bout once. Two categories from one bout make it `mixed`, with the parts listed. A two-handed bout counts once for each arm (3 sets are 3 per arm, not 6). A one-arm bout counts for that arm only. A bout whose side is unknown is reported separately and never added to either arm.
The muscle performs the movement through its range in this exercise (a reviewed direct, dynamic mapping).
The muscle helps move the load but is not the main target (a reviewed contributing, dynamic mapping).
The muscle holds against load in an exercise whose purpose is the hold (hangs, carries, pinches).
The muscle holds or steadies while something else is trained (gripping a bar during a row).
One set loads the muscle in two different ways; it counts once here, with the parts listed.
The mapping exists but its relationship or muscle action is not known.

Grip credit that needs a bare hand is not given to a set logged with straps. Unknown straps keep the credit and say so. Hold seconds are summed per segment and reported as seconds. They are never converted into sets.

Work tagged with the region in the exercise catalog but with no reviewed atlas mapping counts only at region level, never as work for a specific muscle. Draft mappings are shown as pending review and not counted. Unknown is never shown as zero. The region total counts distinct bouts that touched any of its muscles on that arm. It is not the sum of the muscle rows.

Not counted: Sets not logged as completed (typed but not logged, or skipped). Sets marked as warm-ups. Workouts not finished (the live workout's sets count once it is finished). Removed workouts and sets (they no longer exist on the device).
Load × reps is external volume-load, not muscle force.
Effort that was not recorded stays unknown; it never defaults to failure.
Incidental grip is never counted as dynamic work.
No number here predicts growth, recovery or injury.

Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.

muscle: Brachioradialis: Thumb side of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist; the outermost muscle on that edge.
Bends your elbow. It works whichever way the palm faces; anatomy texts describe it as strongest with the thumb pointing up.
Main action · Bends the elbow, bringing the hand toward the shoulder.

Contributes to the thumb-side contour of the upper forearm, the bulge just below the elbow. It does not bend the wrist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
Studies disagree on whether turning the palm up, sideways or down changes how hard it works in a curl.
From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up; that is not counted as a separate action here.

Hammer-style curls keep the forearm in neutral, where the brachioradialis lies well placed to flex the elbow, and they are the usual choice to train it, so it is a direct target here. EMG studies disagree on how much its activity changes with forearm position (M1 found the change in pronation), so 'direct' is a judgement about the exercise's purpose, not a measured larger share.

Brachioradialis bends the elbow and is active whether the palm faces up, sideways or down. Anatomy references describe it as strongest with the forearm half-turned (thumb up). From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up. It does not cross the wrist.

Whether forearm position changes how hard the brachioradialis works when bending the elbow is unsettled. A surface-EMG study of 16 people found its share differed with the palm down compared with palm up or thumb up; a fine-wire EMG study of 10 people found no difference between the three positions. Neither study measured growth.

Brachioradialis is the most superficial muscle on the thumb side of the forearm and forms the fleshy bulge in its upper half, so it may contribute to the thumb-side contour just below the elbow. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

The finger parts of FDS can be recruited selectively to some degree, with coupling between fingers. When one finger flexed at half its maximum force, fewer than half of the motor units serving the other fingers' parts became active, and units serving a neighbouring finger were recruited most readily. This supports describing finger actions; it does not show that one finger's part can be trained in isolation.

Butler, Kilbreath, Gorman and Gandevia, Selective recruitment of single motor units in human flexor digitorum superficialis muscle during flexion of individual fingers (Journal of Physiology, 2005) · Abstract
Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Single-motor-unit recordings during isometric finger flexion in healthy adults.

Ordinary gym grip and finger-flexion exercises load FDS together with the deep finger flexor (FDP). In a video-EMG study of fist making, FDP did most of the work in a light fist and FDS joined in every tight fist, in an order that differed between people. No ordinary exercise has been shown to split the work between them, so the atlas shows it as shared and invents no split.

One logged work set, or one planned set. Each bout has an id; a standard set is one segment. A drop set is one bout. Its stages are segments, each with its own load and reps. It is never counted as several sets.

A muscle counts a bout once. Two categories from one bout make it `mixed`, with the parts listed. A two-handed bout counts once for each arm (3 sets are 3 per arm, not 6). A one-arm bout counts for that arm only. A bout whose side is unknown is reported separately and never added to either arm.
The muscle performs the movement through its range in this exercise (a reviewed direct, dynamic mapping).
The muscle helps move the load but is not the main target (a reviewed contributing, dynamic mapping).
The muscle holds against load in an exercise whose purpose is the hold (hangs, carries, pinches).
The muscle holds or steadies while something else is trained (gripping a bar during a row).
One set loads the muscle in two different ways; it counts once here, with the parts listed.
The mapping exists but its relationship or muscle action is not known.

Grip credit that needs a bare hand is not given to a set logged with straps. Unknown straps keep the credit and say so. Hold seconds are summed per segment and reported as seconds. They are never converted into sets.

Work tagged with the region in the exercise catalog but with no reviewed atlas mapping counts only at region level, never as work for a specific muscle. Draft mappings are shown as pending review and not counted. Unknown is never shown as zero. The region total counts distinct bouts that touched any of its muscles on that arm. It is not the sum of the muscle rows.

Not counted: Sets not logged as completed (typed but not logged, or skipped). Sets marked as warm-ups. Workouts not finished (the live workout's sets count once it is finished). Removed workouts and sets (they no longer exist on the device).
Load × reps is external volume-load, not muscle force.
Effort that was not recorded stays unknown; it never defaults to failure.
Incidental grip is never counted as dynamic work.
No number here predicts growth, recovery or injury.

Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.

muscle: Brachioradialis: Thumb side of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist; the outermost muscle on that edge.
Bends your elbow. It works whichever way the palm faces; anatomy texts describe it as strongest with the thumb pointing up.
Main action · Bends the elbow, bringing the hand toward the shoulder.

Contributes to the thumb-side contour of the upper forearm, the bulge just below the elbow. It does not bend the wrist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
Studies disagree on whether turning the palm up, sideways or down changes how hard it works in a curl.
From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up; that is not counted as a separate action here.

Brachioradialis bends the elbow and is active whether the palm faces up, sideways or down. Anatomy references describe it as strongest with the forearm half-turned (thumb up). From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up. It does not cross the wrist.

Flexor digitorum superficialis is the main muscle bending the four fingers at their middle (PIP) joints. It also helps bend the knuckles (MCP) and the wrist. It has a separate part, with its own tendon, for each finger.

The finger parts of FDS can be recruited selectively to some degree, with coupling between fingers. When one finger flexed at half its maximum force, fewer than half of the motor units serving the other fingers' parts became active, and units serving a neighbouring finger were recruited most readily. This supports describing finger actions; it does not show that one finger's part can be trained in isolation.

Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Single-motor-unit recordings during isometric finger flexion in healthy adults.

Ordinary gym grip and finger-flexion exercises load FDS together with the deep finger flexor (FDP). In a video-EMG study of fist making, FDP did most of the work in a light fist and FDS joined in every tight fist, in an order that differed between people. No ordinary exercise has been shown to split the work between them, so the atlas shows it as shared and invents no split.

One logged work set, or one planned set. Each bout has an id; a standard set is one segment. A drop set is one bout. Its stages are segments, each with its own load and reps. It is never counted as several sets.

A muscle counts a bout once. Two categories from one bout make it `mixed`, with the parts listed. A two-handed bout counts once for each arm (3 sets are 3 per arm, not 6). A one-arm bout counts for that arm only. A bout whose side is unknown is reported separately and never added to either arm.
The muscle performs the movement through its range in this exercise (a reviewed direct, dynamic mapping).
The muscle helps move the load but is not the main target (a reviewed contributing, dynamic mapping).
The muscle holds against load in an exercise whose purpose is the hold (hangs, carries, pinches).
The muscle holds or steadies while something else is trained (gripping a bar during a row).
One set loads the muscle in two different ways; it counts once here, with the parts listed.
The mapping exists but its relationship or muscle action is not known.

Grip credit that needs a bare hand is not given to a set logged with straps. Unknown straps keep the credit and say so. Hold seconds are summed per segment and reported as seconds. They are never converted into sets.

Work tagged with the region in the exercise catalog but with no reviewed atlas mapping counts only at region level, never as work for a specific muscle. Draft mappings are shown as pending review and not counted. Unknown is never shown as zero. The region total counts distinct bouts that touched any of its muscles on that arm. It is not the sum of the muscle rows.

Not counted: Sets not logged as completed (typed but not logged, or skipped). Sets marked as warm-ups. Workouts not finished (the live workout's sets count once it is finished). Removed workouts and sets (they no longer exist on the device).
Load × reps is external volume-load, not muscle force.
Effort that was not recorded stays unknown; it never defaults to failure.
Incidental grip is never counted as dynamic work.
No number here predicts growth, recovery or injury.

Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.

muscle: Brachioradialis: Thumb side of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist; the outermost muscle on that edge.
Bends your elbow. It works whichever way the palm faces; anatomy texts describe it as strongest with the thumb pointing up.
Main action · Bends the elbow, bringing the hand toward the shoulder.

Contributes to the thumb-side contour of the upper forearm, the bulge just below the elbow. It does not bend the wrist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
Studies disagree on whether turning the palm up, sideways or down changes how hard it works in a curl.
From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up; that is not counted as a separate action here.

Brachioradialis bends the elbow and is active whether the palm faces up, sideways or down. Anatomy references describe it as strongest with the forearm half-turned (thumb up). From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up. It does not cross the wrist.

Whether forearm position changes how hard the brachioradialis works when bending the elbow is unsettled. A surface-EMG study of 16 people found its share differed with the palm down compared with palm up or thumb up; a fine-wire EMG study of 10 people found no difference between the three positions. Neither study measured growth.

muscle: Flexor digitorum superficialis: Palm side, middle layer: under the surface wrist flexors and over the deep finger flexor.
Bends your four fingers at their middle joints, and helps bend the knuckles and the wrist. Each finger has its own part of the muscle, but the parts do not work fully apart.
Main action · Bends the four fingers at their middle joints.
Helps · Bends the four fingers at the knuckles.
Helps · Bends the wrist toward the palm.
May add to the general fullness of the palm side of the forearm. It lies under other muscles, so it has no separately visible outline.
Grip and finger-curl work loads it together with the deep finger flexor (FDP); how the work splits between them is not known.

Flexor digitorum superficialis is the main muscle bending the four fingers at their middle (PIP) joints. It also helps bend the knuckles (MCP) and the wrist. It has a separate part, with its own tendon, for each finger.

Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: flexor digitorum superficialis · Quick Facts: Action

The finger parts of FDS can be recruited selectively to some degree, with coupling between fingers. When one finger flexed at half its maximum force, fewer than half of the motor units serving the other fingers' parts became active, and units serving a neighbouring finger were recruited most readily. This supports describing finger actions; it does not show that one finger's part can be trained in isolation.

Butler, Kilbreath, Gorman and Gandevia, Selective recruitment of single motor units in human flexor digitorum superficialis muscle during flexion of individual fingers (Journal of Physiology, 2005) · Abstract
Short-term muscle activity in a controlled task; not a measurement of growth and not a set-credit weight. Single-motor-unit recordings during isometric finger flexion in healthy adults.

Ordinary gym grip and finger-flexion exercises load FDS together with the deep finger flexor (FDP). In a video-EMG study of fist making, FDP did most of the work in a light fist and FDS joined in every tight fist, in an order that differed between people. No ordinary exercise has been shown to split the work between them, so the atlas shows it as shared and invents no split.
